facts: Panda's group helped identify melanopsin, a pigment in certain cells of the eye that responds to blue light and tells the brain's master clock how bright the surroundings are. Papers appeared in Science in 2002, 2003 and 2005.

These cells report brightness, not pictures; a 2003 paper showed the clock-and-light responses in blind mice depend on melanopsin, and the book summaries say the pigment works even in people who are blind or visually impaired.
Light is the strongest time cue for the body clock (zeitgeber).
Blue light at night suppresses melatonin and disrupts sleep; less blue light at night and daylight in the morning help the rhythm line up again.

Panda has led a lab at the Salk Institute in San Diego since 2004; the melanopsin work is cited in research on light therapy for insomnia, ADHD and migraines, and a 2019 Science paper described the functional diversity of these cells in humans.

opening_idea: Start with blind mice whose body clocks still followed the light.

lessons.idea: Your clock reads brightness, so what you look at in the evening can tell your brain it is still daytime.

lessons.example: A student scrolling a bright phone in bed after midnight and one reading on a dim lamp send different signals.
